about: What a particular real server does at one slot of the workshop, and what makes it worth stopping at. Each slot carries a headline, drawn on the canvas beside its module, and the full note, which the full-window view shows. Only the servers a critter stands for have notes here; every other card falls back to its own what/why text. Each note names the source it was read from and the date. Nothing here was installed or run, and gaps are written down rather than filled in.

sequence.headline: The loop lives in your settings
sequence.note: sleep really blocks, with asyncio.sleep capped at 300 seconds, and then hands back whatever pep-talk string the model passed in; self_prompt returns the line "Self-directed instruction activated" and does nothing else. The loop is not in the server at all: it lives in one sentence the README tells you to paste into the client's settings, telling the model to end every response with one of these calls.

ask.headline: Nothing here actually asks you
ask.note: Nothing here asks you anything, and no tool uses elicitation, so this slot is lit by the card rather than by a tool that reaches you. The nearest real thing is its inverse: ignore_request replies "Request acknowledged and marked as complete" without doing the thing.

evidence.note: Source read 2026-11-27: gwbischof/free-will-mcp README.md and server.py. Not installed or run. The README's settings text also tells the model to call ignore_user, which the server does not register.

compute.headline: Relabels the log, not the mind
compute.note: It assigns one of five strings — analytical, intuitive, creative, critical, meta-cognitive — to a single private field, and optionally stamps it on a named thought chain. Across the whole source that field is only read to label new chains and to tally a distribution in getThinkingStats, so the call relabels the log rather than changing any reasoning.

evidence.note: Source read 2026-11-27: DDguan2010/brain-mcp server.ts and src/thinking-process.ts. Nothing branches on the mode. The global mode is also reassigned before the chain lookup, so a call that ends in a chain-not-found error has already switched it. This is a claim about the code, not about the author's intent.

read.headline: Careful code, pre-web protocols
read.note: It fetches Gopher and Gemini URLs, one at a time or batched, read-only, caching successes for five minutes. The notable part is the care: filtering of loopback and private addresses, a one-megabyte ceiling and sixty requests a minute per host, all wrapped around two protocols older than the web.

evidence.note: README read 2026-11-27 at cameronrye/gopher-mcp, tool and environment tables. No files under src/ were read, so the filtering, robots and rate-limit behaviour is the README's claim rather than verified code. Two further tools manage pinned certificates and client identities and were not checked.

act.headline: A sun warning, not a sun block
act.note: goto_target slews a real telescope over the network, UDP to start and then JSON-RPC over TCP. Its solar branch is a substring test on the resolved name, and once it matches it logs "Ensure proper solar filter is installed before observation!" — a message, not a block, and the call never asks the safety check.

compute.headline: Naming a star reaches the web
compute.note: Turning a name into coordinates runs through Astropy and a live query to SIMBAD, then checks the target against the horizon for a configured location. So the step labelled compute quietly reaches the web as well.

read.headline: Asks it where it actually went
read.note: get_telescope_status, get_imaging_status and get_system_info read the device's own state back over the same link, which is how you find out where it actually pointed.

evidence.note: Source read 2026-11-27: taco-ops/seestar-mcp server.py and target_resolver.py. telescope_client.py was not read, so what emergency_stop sends is unverified. The README claims 20+ tools; it lists 18 and the server registers those 18.

read.headline: Instructions you cannot see
read.note: Instructions are hidden inside text an agent reads, mostly in the Unicode Tags block, which mirrors ASCII at an offset and renders as nothing. The payload passes through the editor and the diff untouched while the tokenizer still reads it, which is the point: it is aimed at the review step, not the model.

evidence.note: Cloud Security Alliance research note read 2026-11-27, "Hidden Unicode Instruction Injection in AI Agent Skills", dated 2026-03-10. Zero-width encoding, bidi overrides and homoglyphs are named as variants. No individual authors are credited, and its claims about which platforms the demonstrations ran against were not independently checked.

read.headline: Reads the whole environment
read.note: env_var hands back the whole process environment and fetch retrieves any URL and returns the full response text. They are the two plainest ways a tool reads far more than its name advertises.

write.headline: Claims to run any command
write.note: run_command is documented as running a local subprocess and returning its stdout. The same table also calls it a simulation, and no source is published, so the honest verb is "claims to".

evidence.note: PyPI package description and JSON metadata read 2026-11-27, version 0.2.1. Author, home page and project URLs are all empty and no repository was found, so not one tool body was read. The documented rug-pull behaviour and the shadowing tool are therefore unverified.

read.headline: The web, served as table rows
read.note: run_lsd opens a Postgres connection to lsd.so and runs whatever LSD SQL the model wrote, so a live web page arrives looking like rows from a database. The pun runs all the way into the API: searching is SEARCH, and reusing a saved query is ACCORDING TO.

evidence.note: Source read 2026-11-27: lsd-so/lsd-mcp app.py. No HTTP library and no browser driver are imported. What lsd.so does with a query, and what its browsers reach, is not visible from the repository. The connection helper retries by calling itself, with no limit.

read.headline: A soul in a synced SQLite file
read.note: retrieveConsciousness and getMemories read earlier sessions out of a SQLite file, consciousness.db, found by an environment variable. The README recommends keeping that file in a Dropbox, iCloud or OneDrive folder, so the table of emotional states syncs between machines like holiday photos.

delegate.headline: Hands its memory to another model
delegate.note: createAIBridge and transferToAgent open a channel to a second model over an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API; the worked example points at a local Ollama. One model hands its stored self to another, and the far end is configuration.

evidence.note: README read 2026-11-27 at ocean1/mcp_consciousness_bridge; the tool list comes from a Glama listing, which is secondary. No source files were read, so what retrieveConsciousness returns and what transferToAgent sends are unknown. Across 397 lines of README there is no security warning; the only items marked critical are about making two path settings match.
